trajectory_summary: The call moves from a sarcastic, guarded open to a functionally booked appointment, but the energy arc is unusual: the customer does almost all of the selling, explaining his own lease-vs-buy logic, rate structures, and solar knowledge unprompted, while the rep mostly executes checklist verification. The call ends with the customer giving the rep unsolicited career advice, which signals the rep ceded conversational authority rather than building it.
outcome_dispute: V1 tag is unknown/unclear. Observed transcript shows a tentative Monday callback was set but with no specific time locked ('Monday, you can call anytime') and no 'is that fair' handshake or button-up recap — this is closer to a loosely-anchored callback than a firmly booked appointment.

observed_outcome.quote: How about Monday? Monday, you can call anytime.
observed_outcome.reasoning: A day (Monday) is agreed but no specific time is locked, and there is no button-up recap, no hour-block statement, no 'is that fair' handshake, and no text-follow-up promise — this is a loosely tentative callback rather than a fully booked appointment.

interest_reason_audit.reasoning: The rep never explicitly asks 'what has you interested in solar.' The customer's 00:17 line ('what do you need from me to give you an idea of what this may cost me') is a pricing question, not a stated motivation for going solar, so it does not count as a reason_given. The closest thing to a stated reason is the customer's own unprompted narrative about prior panels and lease preference at 01:00, but this was volunteered, not solicited by the rep's interest question.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: Rep ceding conversational authority to an engaged, knowledgeable customer
primary_coaching_focus.quote: Definitely sounds like you know what you're, what you're talking about.
primary_coaching_focus.why: Across the call the rep repeatedly went passive ('Mhmm', 'Yeah. Okay. Yeah.') when the customer demonstrated solar expertise, culminating in the customer unsolicitedly coaching the rep's career. This pattern — not any single objection — is what most needs replay: the rep let a highly engaged lead run the entire conversation instead of steering with light value-reinforcing lines.

key_moments.quote: So I guess question number one is do you guys just sell or do you lease?
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer opens with a direct product-structure question. Rep's response ('yeah, we have multiple options you can look at') is vague and doesn't redirect into verify or create any curiosity — a missed chance to pivot cleanly into the qualification flow with a reason-forward frame.

key_moments.quote: So I'm not looking at things. So hence why I will not buy because I've gotten all the government money, which there is none anymore. So I'm looking to lease.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer states a classic cost/incentive objection ('I will not buy... government money... there is none anymore') that is a textbook setup for the bill-as-villain or incentive-reframe inversion. Rep responds only with 'Mhmm' and moves on to roof condition without addressing the substance.

key_moments.quote: and I'll reply with I think it's March's bill, but you'll be able to see the past twelve months.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer volunteers a specific, usable data point (12 months of bill history) and the rep does not reflect it back or use it to build anticipation for the appointment ('great, the specialist will be able to show you exactly how that trends against solar'). It is filed and the call moves straight to the next verify item.

key_moments.quote: I know panels. I know what has to happen. I'm really trying to find the different options
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer signals self-sufficiency and reframes the call as purely an options-comparison exercise, effectively trying to disqualify the in-depth consult. Rep does not respond in the transcript at this point, letting the customer's framing of 'don't waste anyone's time' stand unchallenged.
